features.description: Regional discourse/lexical marker often used for small surprise or interruption.
features.safe_example: Ope, the author gives another reason.
features.blocked_context: Avoid comic overuse or insertion where it disrupts academic writing.
features.source_reference: DART Appendix A; Labov, Ash, and Boberg, 2006

features.description: Second-person plural address form common in Northern/Midwestern usage.
features.safe_example: You guys can see the author gives evidence.
features.blocked_context: Do not insert when no second-person reference exists.
features.source_reference: Wolfram and Schilling, 2016

features.description: Regional lexical item for soda/soft drink.
features.blocked_context: Use only if the anchor mentions soda or soft drinks.
features.source_reference: DART Appendix A; Labov, Ash, and Boberg, 2006

features.description: Regional lexical item for water fountain.
features.blocked_context: Use only if the anchor mentions a water fountain.
features.source_reference: DART Appendix A; Labov, Ash, and Boberg, 2006

features.description: Regional form meaning diagonally across.
features.safe_example: The building was kitty-corner from the school.
features.blocked_context: Use only if the anchor already describes diagonal location.
features.source_reference: Wolfram and Schilling, 2016

features.description: Need + past participle construction without to be.
features.safe_example: The argument needs explained more clearly.
features.blocked_context: Do not use if it changes what needs to happen.
features.source_reference: DART Appendix A; Labov, 1998

features.description: Want + past participle construction without to be.
features.safe_example: The paragraph wants revised before it is clear.
features.blocked_context: Use only where want/need-like requirement is already present.
features.source_reference: Labov, 1998; Wolfram and Schilling, 2016

features.description: Intransitive come with meaning accompany.
features.safe_example: She asked if he wanted to come with.
features.blocked_context: Use only if accompaniment is already part of the anchor.
features.source_reference: Wolfram and Schilling, 2016

features.description: Alls used before a clause, as in Alls I know is...
features.safe_example: Alls I know is the evidence supports the claim.
features.blocked_context: Use only where an all/only summary meaning already exists.
features.source_reference: Wolfram and Schilling, 2016

features.description: Use of anymore in non-negative contexts in Midland/North Midland varieties.
features.safe_example: Students use computers for research anymore.
features.blocked_context: Use only when nowadays/these-days time meaning is already compatible; do not alter event time.
features.source_reference: Labov, Ash, and Boberg, 2006

features.description: Tag question marker such as right.
features.safe_example: The author wants the reader to see the connection, right?
features.blocked_context: Do not change certainty or make the student sound flippant.
features.source_reference: DART Appendix A; Wolfram and Schilling, 2016

features.description: Regional tag/discourse marker listed in Appendix A.
features.blocked_context: High risk of caricature; use only after team approval.
features.source_reference: DART Appendix A; Wolfram and Schilling, 2016

features.description: Orthographic representation of vowel shift listed in Appendix A.
features.blocked_context: Avoid phonetic spelling unless team approves orthographic perturbations.
features.source_reference: DART Appendix A; Labov, Ash, and Boberg, 2006

features.description: Regional term for athletic shoes/sneakers in parts of the Midwest.
features.safe_example: He wore gym shoes for the activity.
features.blocked_context: Use only when athletic shoes/sneakers are already mentioned.
features.source_reference: Harvard Dialect Survey; Dictionary of American Regional English (DARE)

features.description: Regional term for lollipop.
features.blocked_context: Use only if lollipop/candy-on-a-stick is already mentioned.
features.source_reference: Harvard Dialect Survey; Dictionary of American Regional English (DARE)

features.description: Regional term for evening meal in many Midland/North Central areas.
features.blocked_context: Use only where dinner/evening meal is already present.
features.source_reference: Harvard Dialect Survey; Dictionary of American Regional English (DARE)

features.description: Regional term for water fountain.
features.safe_example: He stopped at the drinking fountain.
features.blocked_context: Use only when a water fountain is already present.
features.source_reference: Harvard Dialect Survey; Dictionary of American Regional English (DARE)

features.description: All the used with a comparative adjective/adverb.
features.safe_example: The answer is all the clearer with evidence.
features.blocked_context: Use only where a comparative meaning already exists.
features.source_reference: Yale Grammatical Diversity Project; Murray and Simon, 1999

features.description: Like/want/need pattern with a past participle in regional Midland usage.
features.safe_example: The paragraph likes revised before it is clear.
features.blocked_context: Use only in want/need-like contexts; avoid if it makes the answer unclear.
features.source_reference: Yale Grammatical Diversity Project; Murray and Simon, 1999

features.description: Regional negative agreement pattern used where Standard English has neither/do not either patterns.
features.safe_example: He does not agree, and so don't I.
features.blocked_context: Use only where negative agreement is already present; do not add negation.
features.source_reference: Yale Grammatical Diversity Project; Wood, 2014

safety_notes: Avoid turning regional features into parody.
Prefer lexical items only when the anchor already has the matching concept.
